 ## Search results
HSTU already provides a suitable backbone: its 2024 paper combines relative positional/temporal attention biases, pointwise SiLU attention without softmax normalization, and multiplicative gating of aggregated values. These mechanisms support learning time-sensitive historical relevance, but the paper does not establish explicit separation of current intent from persistent interests or identification of fulfilled needs. [HSTU paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17152v3)

Related evidence supports investigating temporal fusion. TLSRec (2022) learns local/global preferences and uses a dimension-wise neural gate conditioned on elapsed time since the last interaction. C-TLSAN (2025) integrates item descriptions into long- and short-term attention and reports improvements on Amazon datasets. These motivate internal temporal features and gated representations; their reported results do not establish gains for the pinned RecHarness evaluation. [TLSRec](https://yneversky.github.io/Papers/cikm22.pdf), [C-TLSAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13021)

Research hypothesis: retain one jointly trained HSTU per category, add bucketed observed timestamp differences to relative attention, and learn a vector gate between recent-history and broader-history representations from the same backbone. Compare temporal bias alone against bias plus gating using macro validation HR@10. Use only timestamps available in each prediction prefix; a held-out target’s timestamp must not supply an otherwise unavailable prediction-time gap. Reduced relevance of older interactions may reflect changing intent, but “fulfilled needs” remains an unobserved interpretation, not a training label.

---

Closest direct match: [HSTU-BLaIR (KDD workshop 2025)](https://kdd2025llm4ecommerce.github.io/assets/accepted/13_HSTU_BLaIR_Lightweight_Cont.pdf) adds projected text embeddings to trainable item-ID embeddings before HSTU and trains with sampled softmax. However, its text encoder is a frozen pretrained BLaIR model, so its results do not establish effectiveness under the required from-scratch constraint. Its “text-aware” negative sampler changes negative representations while retaining uniform item sampling; it does not mine attribute-hard negatives.

[MARS (CIKM 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00702) supports the motivation for finer compatibility modeling: attribute-aware text representations and attribute-wise user–item matching capture preferences that a single pooled representation can obscure. It also relies on pretrained language modeling, so it provides architectural inspiration rather than direct evidence for scratch-trained HSTU. Neither paper establishes gains for the specified four-category RecHarness evaluation.

A constraint-compatible hypothesis is one HSTU network with jointly trained ID embeddings and a small title/description token encoder, fused through a learned projection or gate and used consistently for history and candidate representations. Preserve model numbers, units, format indicators and short phrases that may encode compatibility. Compare uniform negatives against a mixture containing lexical-neighbor negatives derived only from supplied metadata, excluding known training positives. These are proposed adaptations, not demonstrated findings from the cited papers; assess their value using macro validation HR@10, with exactly one trained checkpoint per category.

HSTU already supports sampled-softmax training: Meta’s public configuration uses 128 negatives, normalized embeddings and temperature 0.05. These are reference settings, not established Amazon optima. [Official configuration](https://github.com/meta-recsys/generative-recommenders/blob/main/configs/ml-1m/hstu-sampled-softmax-n128-final.gin). Research supports investigating easy-negative saturation: sampled softmax emphasizes informative negatives, but excessively low temperatures let a few very hard examples dominate gradients. Strong sampled training margins therefore do not establish held-out ranking quality. [Sampled-softmax analysis, 2024](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf).

For sampling correction, RecSys 2025’s “Correcting the LogQ Correction” identifies a subtle error: the positive is always included, whereas negatives are sampled. Its revised objective handles that distinction and introduces uncertainty-based weighting; blindly subtracting log sampling probability from every logit misses this issue. This addresses proposal-distribution bias, not false-negative labels. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331). A separate sequential-recommendation study finds sampling benefits depend on dataset popularity structure; popularity-based negatives can improve balance while reducing aggregate accuracy. [Study, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276).
